set.hook: The one-star table set into the arches of the city wall above the Old Port, dinner only, tasting menus.
set.why: The dining room is built into the vaulted casemates of the wall at Sv. Dominika, and the tables run along the top of the fortification over the harbour, so the weather decides more than the kitchen does. Marijo Curić cooks Adriatic fish and shellfish with Asian seasoning and French technique. In 2026 it is the only Dubrovnik address with a MICHELIN star, and Gault&Millau Croatia 2026 gives it 18/20, the joint top score in the country.
set.verdict: The grand night on this coast, and the one booking to make first. The cooking is precise rather than loud, and the setting does half the work. It is also the house most exposed to the calendar and the wind: it runs a spring-to-autumn season and a Jugo can move dinner indoors. Book the wall tables, accept the price, and check it is still trading before you promise it to guests late in the year.
set.signature: The long tasting menu, taken on the wall terrace at sunset
set.caveat: Seasonal and dinner only, closed Mondays; 2026 closing date not published in what we found, so call before promising it after mid-October

set.hook: A MICHELIN-selected kitchen stacked through a Prijeko townhouse, from street terrace to a small rooftop.
set.why: Prijeko Palace is a 15th-century townhouse on the street that runs parallel to the Stradun, now a nine-room boutique hotel. Its restaurant uses the building vertically: a terrace on the street, a dining room on the third floor and a small rooftop above the tiled roofs. The kitchen keeps a Croatian wine cellar and cooks Mediterranean food that MICHELIN has listed since 2017 and still lists in the Croatia 2026 selection.
set.verdict: Prijeko is the street of menu-touts, and this is the address on it that a guide can send people to without apology. Go for the rooftop, which is small and books out, and treat the street terrace as a fallback. The cooking is careful rather than daring. The hotel shut from early January to the end of February in 2026, so winter plans need a call.

set.hook: Classic Dalmatian-French cooking on two sea terraces at Pile, in the city's 1881 nautical school.
set.why: The building at Brsalje 3, just outside the Pile Gate, opened in 1881 as Dubrovnik's school of navigation, and the terraces look straight across the water at the Lovrijenac and Bokar fortresses. Mario Bunda's kitchen applies French and Italian technique to Dalmatian fish and shellfish. Gault&Millau Croatia 2026 rates it 16.5/20 as a 'remarkable restaurant', and MICHELIN keeps it in the 2026 selection with a four-coin price band.
set.verdict: The safe grand dinner: white tablecloths, set pieces done properly, a view that sells itself. It does not try to surprise, and at these prices some guests will want it to. For a principal who wants the classic Dubrovnik evening without a tasting-menu marathon, this is the booking. Check the season: listings put it on a spring-to-October calendar.

set.caveat: Book the sea terrace two weeks ahead; season appears to end around late October, call before planning November

set.hook: An 1886 fish house off the Stradun, still grilling Adriatic fish all year with a winter schedule.
set.why: Proto has cooked fish in the same lane off the Stradun since 1886, and the old record keeps its best story: the future Edward VIII ate here with Wallis Simpson in 1936. It is now run by the Esculap group, which also owns Konavoski Dvori, and it is one of the few Old Town kitchens that stays open through the winter. Gault&Millau Croatia 2026 scores it 14.5/20, and MICHELIN keeps it in the selection.
set.verdict: The reliable fish dinner inside the walls, and in late autumn one of the few that is certain to be open. Expect the classics cooked properly rather than any surprise, and prices set for the Stradun. Ask for the terrace at lunch; the indoor rooms are better than they look from the lane. Good choice for a crew night out or a last-minute table this week.

set.hook: Old Ragusan recipes on the Jesuit square, built around the capon the house is named after.
set.why: Kopun means capon, a castrated cockerel, and the restaurant took both its name and its point from the bird, which turns up in the city's Renaissance comedies of Marin Držić. The house cooks it slowly with orange and honey and serves it on Poljana Ruđera Boškovića, the square at the top of the Jesuit stairs. Falstaff's Croatia 2026 guide gives it 86 points and singles out the vegetarian dishes as well as the capon.
set.verdict: Worth the climb for dishes the rest of the Old Town does not cook, and the square is quieter than the streets below it. Order the capon and the šporki makaruli and skip the international side of the menu. Mid-priced for the walls. Winter opening is not confirmed in what we found, so call before building a November plan around it.

set.hook: A walk-in charcoal grill high in the Old Town under a vine roof, closed now until spring.
set.why: The grill sits near the top of the Old Town under the northern wall, an open charcoal fire in a corner and a terrace roofed in vines with the roofs falling away below. set.hook: A family konoba in Bosanka on Srđ, ten minutes up from the walls, cooking peka to order.
set.why: Bosanka is a hamlet on Srđ, the ridge behind the city, and the konoba is a ten-minute drive up the hairpins. Its point is peka: lamb, veal or octopus sealed under an iron bell and buried in embers, which takes hours and has to be ordered by phone. Guides differ on the notice needed, from three to four hours. On the way down the terrace looks back over Lokrum and the islands.
set.verdict: The easiest proper peka from a Dubrovnik berth, and worth the planning. Book the table and the bell together, a day ahead if you can. The rest of the menu is ordinary; the peka is why you go. We found no 2026-dated evidence of trading or winter hours, and the phone number differs between sources, so confirm before sending guests up the hill.

set.hook: An old watermill on the Ljuta in Konavle, serving river trout, frog brodet and peka in the woods.
set.why: The restaurant occupies a restored watermill on the Ljuta, a cold spring river that drops through woodland in Konavle, the valley south of Cavtat towards Montenegro. The water runs past the terraces and through the old mill race. Staff wear Konavle costume, and the kitchen cooks what the valley cooks: trout from the river, frogs in brodet, lamb under the bell. It has fed families from Dubrovnik for generations.
set.verdict: A lunch outing rather than a dinner, best combined with a drive through Konavle or a day at Cavtat. The costumes lean towards folklore, but the frog brodet and the trout are real local food you will not find in town. We found no 2026-dated evidence and no current MICHELIN listing, so confirm hours by phone, especially in winter.

set.hook: The Šare family's oyster house in a vaulted Mali Ston salt store, the root of a Croatian chain.
set.why: Božidar Šare, known as Bota, opened this restaurant in Mali Ston with his wife Tanja a few decades ago, in a vaulted stone building by the harbour that was once a salt store. The family's farming and fishing ties to the bay explain the menu. From here the name spread to oyster and sushi bars in Dubrovnik, Split and Zagreb, which still take fish and shellfish from Mali Ston daily.
set.verdict: The more polished of the two Mali Ston houses, and the safer pick for guests: vaulted room, sea view, oysters opened to order a few metres from the beds. The sushi side is a modern addition rather than a local tradition; stay with the oysters and shellfish. Listings say it trades all year, which makes it one of the few out-of-town tables to plan in November.

set.hook: The old family oyster house on Mali Ston bay, with seawater tanks on the terrace and rooms upstairs.
set.why: Vila Koruna bills itself as the oldest eating house in the area and has been serving Mali Ston oysters since 1973. Its shellfish and fish wait in stone tanks on the terrace, glass-fronted and filled with seawater drawn from 48 metres down. A Valamar writer counted oysters done eleven ways, from raw with wild orange to fried and in soup. There are six guest rooms above the dining room.
set.verdict: The plainer, older-feeling of the two Mali Ston houses, good for oysters, mussels and a long lunch by the water without ceremony. Fine for a Pelješac overnight. We found no 2026-dated evidence that it is trading and no winter hours, so this one needs a phone call before it goes on any guest list.

set.hook: Bosnian family kitchen inside the walls, MICHELIN Bib Gourmand, grilled meat from its own butcher.
set.why: The name has nothing to do with India: this is the Old Town's Bosnian house, on Nikole Gučetića just off the Stradun. MICHELIN lists it as a Bib Gourmand and says the meat on the grill comes from the family's own butcher, and the plum baklava is made by the owner's mother. There is a second, roomier branch in Hotel Lero, a few kilometres up toward Gruž, for nights the alley is full.
set.verdict: Good-value Balkan cooking with a guide's backing, in a part of town where value is rare. Expect meat, kajmak and bread in quantity, not seafood. Book: the small room fills, and MICHELIN itself advises reservations. A sound last-minute table for crew or guests who are tired of grilled fish.

set.hook: Wood-fired pizzeria between the Ploče gate and the cable car, cheap beer and very large panzerotti.
set.why: Tabasco sits on Hvarska, the lane that climbs from outside the eastern walls toward the cable-car station, which is why locals rather than day-trippers fill it. Lonely Planet notes the pizzas come out of a wood oven and that it does takeaway and delivery when the terrace is full; In Your Pocket says the beer is among the cheapest near the Old Town. set.verdict: A plain, honest pizzeria, not a destination: Time Out gives it three stars out of five and calls it standard, and that is fair. Its value is being open late, every day, a short walk from the walls, at prices well under the Stradun. Send crew here after service, or guests who want pizza without a scene.

set.hook: Old Town wine bar off the Stradun pouring Croatian bottles by the glass and in tasting flights.
set.why: D'vino sits on Palmotićeva, one of the stepped lanes north of the Stradun, and was built around one idea: let a visitor taste the country without buying bottles. The bar's own site claims more than 60 wines by the glass, the largest such list in Dubrovnik, and the flights of Croatian whites and reds come with English notes. Total Croatia News names Sasha Lušić as the owner who runs the room.
set.verdict: The most efficient way to learn Pelješac, Korčula and Konavle wine in one sitting before the dinners and cellar visits. It is a bar, small plates at most, and tourist-facing by design, so it runs on the season. Check it is still open before building a late-October aperitivo around it.
set.signature: A flight of Croatian reds built around Plavac Mali.
set.caveat: Seasonal per Total Croatia News (about April–late October); may already be closed for winter, call first.

set.hook: Mike Grgich's Pelješac homecoming above Trstenik: two wines, Plavac Mali and Pošip, tasted side by side.
set.why: Miljenko Grgich left Croatia, made the Chardonnay that won the 1976 Paris tasting, and came back in 1996 to build a winery on the headland above Trstenik. It still makes just two wines, and the tasting covers both. Falstaff tasted them in April 2026 and gave the 2022 Plavac Mali and the 2024 Pošip 93 points each, and lists the house in its 2026 guide.
set.verdict: A short, focused visit rather than a long estate tour: two glasses, a view over the Trstenik bay and a story every wine-minded guest will know. Pair it with lunch on Pelješac. Outside July and August the family-run schedule can slip, and nobody may be free to guide you; ring first.
set.signature: The Plavac Mali next to the Pošip.
set.caveat: Call ahead outside peak season; Time Out gives April–November only.

set.hook: The Miloš family's organic Plavac Mali house at Ponikve, maker of Stagnum, tasted in a rock-cut room.
set.why: Above Ston at Ponikve, the Miloš family farms Plavac Mali organically and ages its top red, Stagnum, in large old Slavonian oak. Hugh Johnson called it the first Croatian cult wine. Falstaff's Peter Moser tasted the 2016 in April 2026, scored it 94 and called it a traditional icon of the peninsula. The tasting room is built into the rock of the hillside.
set.verdict: The serious red stop on Pelješac, for guests who want to taste aged Plavac Mali rather than the fresh style. Tastings are quiet and unhurried. Fit it on the way back from Ston oysters; book in advance, since this is a family house, not a visitor centre.
set.caveat: Book ahead; listed hours are undated and 2026 tasting prices were not found.

set.hook: Gruž harbour's open market and fish hall, where boats from the Elafiti land the morning catch.
set.why: On the Gruž waterfront, opposite the ferry and cruise berths, the city's working market sells produce from the Konavle and Rijeka Dubrovačka growers outdoors and fish under cover. Time Out says the fish comes in from the Elafiti islands and to arrive by seven for the best of it. Absolute Croatia says Friday and Saturday are the busiest days, and that prices soften toward closing.
set.verdict: The provisioning stop for any boat lying in Gruž: real fish, real vegetables, cash in hand. Go early, because the fish hall thins out fast. Do not expect a food hall; it is a market for buying, not for eating.
set.signature: The morning's fish from the Elafiti boats.
set.caveat: Cash only on most stalls; come before 07:00 for fish; hours conflict across listings.

set.hook: A tiny Old Town sandwich counter: warm house bread, Drniš pršut and Konavle cheese, in Gault&Millau 2026.
set.why: On Antuninska, a stepped lane off the Stradun, Škola does one thing: a sandwich on bread baked in the house, filled with pršut from Drniš in the Dalmatian hinterland and cheese from Konavle south of the city. It made both the Gault&Millau Croatia 2026 and Falstaff 2026 guides, the latter at 82 points, which is rare for a place with three tables. There is a special menu with vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free choices.
set.verdict: The best cheap lunch inside the walls and the quickest: order, eat standing or take it to the harbour. It is not a restaurant and does not pretend to be. Good for crew between jobs and for guests who want one honest local bite between the walls walk and the boat.
set.signature: The pršut and Konavle cheese sandwich on warm house bread.
set.caveat: Three tables only; hours and phone vary across listings.

set.hook: Old Town seafood counter off the Stradun turning the day's catch into octopus burgers and anchovy sandwiches.
set.why: Barba, Dalmatian for uncle, takes local fish and puts it in a bun: octopus burger, shrimp and tuna burgers, anchovy sandwiches, fried calamari, shrimp tacos, and an octopus sandwich with mascarpone. It is a counter with a few seats on Boškovićeva, a narrow lane a minute from the Stradun. A Wanderlog list updated in November 2025 still counted it among the city's street-food stops.
set.verdict: Worth one visit for the octopus burger, which most reviewers praise; past that the record is mixed, with complaints of heavy batter and a poor shrimp burger. Fast, cheap by Old Town standards, crowded at peak. Go off-hours and keep it to the octopus.
set.caveat: No 2026-dated evidence; hours conflict and winter opening unknown; call +385 91 205 3488.
